The Austral parakeet Enicognathus ferrugineus begins its life cycle with a relatively small investment per offspring. Field studies conducted in the subantarctic forests of Tierra del Fuego have documented that newly hatched chicks emerge from eggs weighing approximately 9.77 grams [Wwb = approximately 9.77 grams], a value consistent with the altricial mode of development typical of most Psittacidae. The incubation period is notably sensitive to environmental conditions; eggs incubated under controlled conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after an average of 27.2 days [ab = 27.2 days], a duration that reflects the thermal constraints on embryonic development in a cool-temperate climate. Immediately following hatching, the downy chicks are brooded intensively by both parents, and the initial wet weight of the neonate, measured as 10.46 grams [Ww0 = 10.46 grams], represents the post-absorptive body mass after yolk sac resorption. This early mass provides the foundation for a rapid growth phase that will continue through the nestling period.

As the nestling chicks progress toward independence, they undergo a period of sustained mass gain under the thermal regime typical of brooding adults. At a body temperature of approximately 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], which is characteristic of active homeothermy in this species, the developmental sequence unfolds in a predictable manner. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight capability, occurs at 54 days after hatching [tx = 54 days after hatching], a milestone that coincides with the full emergence of flight feathers and the ability to leave the nest cavity at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. The timing of this event is critical for avoiding predation and for synchronizing with peak food availability. During the latter part of the nestling phase, the chicks experience a substantial increase in body mass, eventually reaching the adult asymptotic mass of 166.95 grams [Wwi = 166.95 grams], which is maintained through the juvenile period and into adulthood.

Sexual maturation in Enicognathus ferrugineus represents a significant life-history transition that occurs well after the achievement of adult body size. Under the same thermal conditions maintained during the active metabolic period at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], puberty, characterized by the onset of gonadal activity and gametogenesis, is attained at 162 days after hatching [tp = 162 days after hatching]. This relatively protracted juvenile phase is likely an adaptation to the challenges of learning complex foraging techniques, such as extracting seeds from Araucaria cones. Following the attainment of sexual maturity, individuals do not breed immediately; instead, the first successful nesting attempt typically occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], a one-year delay that may reflect the time required to establish a territory and secure a mate within the dense Nothofagus forests of southern South America at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C].

The reproductive output of the Austral parakeet is constrained by both its slow pace of life and the harsh subantarctic environment it inhabits. Females typically produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], which represents a low annual reproductive frequency compared to many small passerines. Each clutch contains approximately 5 to 6 eggs [N_R_i = Each clutch contains approximately 5 to 6 eggs], yielding a modest annual fecundity that is balanced by the extended biparental care provided to the altricial chicks. The maximum reproductive rate recorded under ideal conditions, observed in captive colonies where food was provided ad libitum, was 5.7 eggs per year [Ri = 5.7 eggs per year], a value that underscores the species' conservative life-history strategy. This low reproductive output is complemented by a relatively long potential lifespan; maximum longevity in the wild, inferred from banding studies, reaches approximately 15.2 years [am = approximately 15.2 years] under the thermal conditions typical of the species' active metabolic period at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C].

Comparisons with other South American parrots reveal the ecological specialization of Enicognathus ferrugineus. Its adult body mass of 166.95 grams [Wwi = 166.95 grams] places it among the medium-sized members of the Arini tribe, somewhat larger than the sympatric Monk parakeet but smaller than the larger macaws. The species' dawn choruses and flocking behavior are well documented, with groups of up to several dozen birds foraging on seeds, berries, and leaf buds. Studies of foraging ecology indicate that the birds are highly dependent on the mast of southern beeches and the fleshy fruits of endemic shrubs. The mortality regime is characterized by occasional predation by forest falcons and other raptors, as well as by harsh winter conditions that may cause significant mortality among first-year birds. Despite these pressures, the maximum lifespan of 15.2 years [am = 15.2 years] is notable for a parrot of this size and indicates a relatively slow pace of life that is typical of long-lived tropical and subtropical psittacines at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C].
